analysis.one_liner: Forces big meatpackers to buy a share of cattle at openly negotiated prices and publish their contract terms.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and never advanced, dying without a vote at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Agriculture Department to set regional minimum percentages of cattle that big meatpackers must buy through open, negotiated deals rather than private formula contracts, and to publish a public library of the contracts packers offer to cattle producers, including premiums, discounts, and price terms. Its goal was to restore "price discovery" — letting the market visibly set cattle prices — in a market where four large packers buy most cattle through confidential arrangements. The bill never received a hearing vote or floor action; it sat in the House Agriculture Committee until the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Cattle ranchers and feedlot operators gain because more of their cattle would be bought at prices openly negotiated at the time of sale, instead of priced later off formulas set by the packer — giving them real leverage and visibility into the terms packers offer. Consumers ultimately benefit too: when packers can quietly price cattle off their own formula contracts, the prices ranchers receive (and eventually what shoppers pay) are less tied to a genuine market.

how_it_helps.text: USDA must set regional minimum percentages of cattle that meat packers must buy through open, negotiated transactions, so more prices are set in a visible market rather than by formula contracts.
USDA must create and publish a library of every type of contract packers offer to cattle producers, including premiums, discounts, delivery commitments, and the number of cattle committed.

Packers must report prior-day slaughter schedules over a 14-day window, base prices paid on formula contracts, and carcass weights must be reported on an expedited schedule, giving producers and markets more current information.

analysis.who_pays: The four large meatpacking companies that dominate cattle slaughter would bear the cost: they would have to buy a mandated share of cattle through negotiated trades, disclose their contract terms publicly, and report more purchase data — reducing their pricing control and adding compliance costs, some of which they might pass along to consumers.

drawbacks.text: Requiring packers to buy a set share of cattle through open negotiation raises their procurement costs and reduces their pricing flexibility, costs that could be passed on to consumers in the form of higher beef prices.

The bill relied on USDA rulemaking to set regional minimums, with a notice-and-comment process and a two-year cost-benefit review, so the actual stringency of the mandate would have been determined by regulators after passage and could have been set weakly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — forcing a share of cattle to be traded at openly negotiated prices — would cost the four large meatpackers some pricing control and could raise packing costs that show up partly in beef prices; the strongest good-faith objection is that government-set purchase quotas could disrupt efficient contracting. But ranchers and consumers alike pay today when a thin cash market lets packers anchor prices to their own captive supplies, and the bill kept its mandate modest (initially no more than the recent regional average of negotiated sales). On balance the transparency and price-discovery provisions were a measured response to a real concentration problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and its livestock subcommittee and never came up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 17, 2021 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture.
On December 2, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture, and no further action followed.
The bill had six Republican cosponsors in addition to its Democratic sponsor, showing bipartisan support that never translated into floor action.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies keep their current pricing arrangements and reporting obligations unchanged, since no minimum negotiated-purchase share or contract library was ever enacted.

for.name: Rep. Cynthia Axne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to mandate negotiated-purchase minimums and a public cattle contract library.

for.name: Reps. Feenstra, Hinson, Miller-Meeks, Hartzler, and Fortenberry
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the bill six Republican cosponsors alongside its Democratic sponsor.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral; the bill never received a markup or floor vote.

against.name: Meatpacking industry
against.role: Four large beef packers processing the majority of fed cattle
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed mandated minimum levels of negotiated cattle purchases during the period, arguing they would raise costs without fixing prices.

sides.party_line_note: A House Democrat introduced the bill and six Republicans cosponsored it — members from cattle-feeding states of both parties backed it — yet it received no committee or floor action.

industries.industry: Large meatpacking companies (the four-firm majority of fed cattle slaughter)
industries.note: The bill would force them to buy a set share of cattle at openly negotiated prices and disclose their contract terms and purchase plans. It attacks the pricing leverage that comes from buying most cattle through their own long-term formulas.
More negotiated trades mean real market prices for cattle and public visibility into contract terms, improving the leverage of producers who today sell against packer-set formulas.
